identity.title: AS1411-targeted nanomedicines for precision cancer therapy: Advances, mechanisms, and translational perspectives.

content.abstract: Conventional cancer chemotherapy is frequently compromised by nonspecific biodistribution, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, inadequate tumor accumulation, and multidrug resistance, highlighting the need for targeted nanomedicines capable of improving tumor selectivity while preserving therapeutic efficacy. The AS1411 G-quadruplex DNA aptamer has emerged as a promising targeting ligand owing to its high affinity for nucleolin, which is aberrantly overexpressed on the surface of many malignant cells. AS1411-functionalized nanocarriers can exploit nucleolin-mediated endocytosis to enhance tumor-cell uptake, intracellular drug delivery, and therapeutic selectivity while minimizing off-target exposure. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AS1411-engineered nanocarriers, encompassing polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, liposomes, inorganic and mesoporous nanostructures, as well as bioinspired platforms such as exosomes and cell membrane-coated nanoparticles. Particular emphasis is placed on rational nanocarrier engineering, including optimization of AS1411 surface density, PEGylation, physicochemical properties, and integration of tumor microenvironment-responsive mechanisms to achieve controlled and stimuli-responsive payload release. These platforms have been explored for the targeted delivery of conventional chemotherapeutics, nucleic acid therapeutics, and nonviral CRISPR/Cas systems, and increasingly incorporate multimodal therapeutic and diagnostic functions, including photothermal, photodynamic, sonodynamic, chemodynamic, and imaging-guided approaches. Despite considerable progress, clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous nucleolin expression, complex tumor microenvironmental barriers, limited endosomal escape and intracellular trafficking, potential off-target interactions, formulation stability, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory challenges. Future development should prioritize mechanistic understanding of AS1411-nucleolin interactions, standardized evaluation of targeting efficiency, and rational integration of multi-responsive, dual- and multi-ligand, and bioinspired architectures. Such advances may improve the translational potential of AS1411-based nanomedicines and support their further preclinical development.
